# Vidhurajātaka (Ja 546)

**ID:** Ja 546
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Vidhurajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Vidhura the Wise of Kuru
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja546
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vidhurajātaka* (numbered as Ja 546 in the Burmese Chatthasaṅgāyana tradition and SuttaCentral, though often cited as Ja 545 in European scholarship) is one of the celebrated "ten great *jātaka*s" (*mahājātaka*) forming the climax of the canonical collection [SuttaCentral; Wood 2005; Appleton 2010a]. The story is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the tale concerning his past perfection of wisdom or truthfulness [SuttaCentral; Cunningham 1879; Appleton 2010b]. In the narrative, the Bodhisatta is born as Vidhura (or Vidhurapaṇḍita), a wise minister and counsellor to King Dhanañjaya Koravya of Indapatta in the Kuru realm [Appleton 2012; Cunningham 1879]. Coveted for his wisdom by a nāga queen, Vidhura is abducted by the yakkha Puṇṇaka; rather than succumbing to fear, the Bodhisatta instructs the yakkha in the Dhamma and subdues him atop Mount Kāḷagiri through his superior wisdom [Appleton 2012; Anandajoti 2010; Cunningham 1879]. In the closing identification (*samodhāna*), King Dhanañjaya is revealed to be Ānanda, the nāga and garuḷa kings are Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Sakka is Anuruddha, and Vidhura's son is Rāhula [Appleton 2012].

The text has long enjoyed immense cultural and artistic prominence. Visual depictions include a detailed nine-scene narration on a corner return pillar at the 3rd-century BCE Bharhut stūpa (inscribed as *viturapunakiyajatakam*) and late 5th-century CE murals in Cave 2 at Ajanta [Wood 2005; Cunningham 1879; Spink 2009]. Textually, a verse found in the Burmese recension is shared with the *Milindapañha* [von Hinüber 1994], and the tale is referenced in the *Vimānavatthu* (Vv 84), *Petavatthu* (Pv 21, Pv 37), and *Milindapañha* (Mil 7.2.8) [SuttaCentral]. Curated passage parallels exist with several other canonical Jātakas, notably the *Saṅkhapālajātaka* (Ja 524), *Bhūripaññajātaka* (Ja 452), and *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538), with resembling narratives in the *Mahāvastu* and *Sūcijātaka* (Ja 387) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse algorithms in DharmaNexus confirm substantial verse sharing across the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Dhammanīti*, *Naradakkhadīpanī*, and Ja 524, alongside cross-language alignments with the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (D0006), Kṣemendra's *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā*, the Tibetan *Jātakamālā*, and the *Nāgarājābherīgāthā* [DharmaNexus].
